item.title: Cancer cases continue to rise as Fiji Cancer Society registers about 217 since January
item.description: Since January this year, 217 people have turned to the Fiji Cancer Society after being diagnosed with cancer, a number that continues to rise year after year. Fiji Cancer Society Board member Inoke Bainimarama highlighted this during their Annual 5KM Pink Walk at Albert Park this morning, saying the event is not just a walk but an important platform for raising awareness.
item.content:encoded:
Since January this year, 217 people have turned to the Fiji Cancer Society after being diagnosed with cancer, a number that continues to rise year after year.

Fiji Cancer Society Board member Inoke Bainimarama highlighted this during their Annual 5KM Pink Walk at Albert Park this morning, saying the event is not just a walk but an important platform for raising awareness.

Bainimarama says this year’s theme is “Turning Awareness into Action”, and he acknowledged everyone who turned up to support the cause.

More than 270 people, young and old, braved the rainy Suva weather this morning to take part in the walk, while another 220 people participated simultaneously in Lautoka.

He says they were delighted to have sponsors and more than 15 organisations represented at the event, as well as students, including members of the Suva Grammar School First XV.

Bainimarama also acknowledged cancer survivors who participated in the walk, saying they are at the forefront of the Society’s advocacy work.

He says they want to use the month of October to draw greater attention to cancer and raise awareness, particularly about breast cancer.

item.title: Fiji prepares for evolving terrorism and security threats with launch of Counter Terrorism Strategy 2026–2030
item.description: Fiji is stepping up preparations to address terrorism and emerging security threats, despite the Government saying a terrorist attack remains unlikely in the foreseeable future. This is at the centre of Fiji’s new Counter Terrorism Strategy 2026–2030, launched at the Grand Pacific Hotel in Suva.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji is stepping up preparations to address terrorism and emerging security threats, despite the Government saying a terrorist attack remains unlikely in the foreseeable future.

This is at the centre of Fiji’s new Counter Terrorism Strategy 2026–2030, launched at the Grand Pacific Hotel in Suva.

Minister for Policing and Communications Ioane Naivalurua says Fiji must prepare while the country remains at peace, stressing that unlikely does not mean impossible.

Naivalurua says the nature of terrorism and violent extremism has changed, with radicalisation able to occur online, extremist ideas spreading rapidly and violence potentially emerging from individual grievances with little warning.

He says the strategy is about protecting Fiji’s people, communities and institutions, while preserving the peace for future generations.

Naivalurua says Fiji will not tolerate terrorism or violent extremism from any direction, regardless of ideology, motivation or justification.

However, he says counterterrorism measures must remain principled and cannot become a basis for discrimination or suspicion based on religion, ethnicity, village, language or belief.

Naivalurua say Fiji’s response will remain grounded in the Constitution, rule of law, human rights, due process, necessity, proportionality and accountability.

He says counterterrorism is not simply a policing responsibility but a national responsibility, requiring cooperation between government agencies, security institutions, communities, schools, traditional and faith leaders, financial institutions, the technology sector and international partners.

The strategy is built around four pillars - prevention, preparation, response and recovery.

Naivalurua says prevention will focus on identifying and reducing risks before they become threats, while preparation will ensure government, security agencies and critical sectors are ready before a crisis occurs.

He says response will focus on protecting life, containing threats and restoring public safety, while recovery will involve restoring confidence, supporting affected communities and learning from incidents.

Naivalurua says the Government is also developing a Counterterrorism and Suppression of Terrorism Financing Bill with relevant agencies and international partners.

He says the legislation will strengthen Fiji’s legal capacity while ensuring counterterrorism action remains consistent with the Constitution, rule of law and human rights.

Naivalurua says Fiji’s security is also closely linked to the wider Pacific, with the country continuing to work with regional neighbours and international partners on intelligence sharing, border security, financial intelligence, cyber resilience and operational cooperation.

Meanwhile, US Embassy Chargé d’Affaires Christina Cavallo says threats today cross borders and increasingly move online, making preparedness a shared responsibility.

Cavallo says no single agency can address these threats alone, with security requiring cooperation across government, law enforcement, faith and community leaders, the private sector and international partners.

She says the new strategy is more than a policy document, describing it as a statement of national resolve and a contribution to regional security.

Cavallo says the United States recognises Fiji’s leadership and is proud to stand alongside Fiji as it strengthens its counterterrorism framework.

She says the United States has provided significant support to Fiji in areas linked to security and resilience.

This includes US$500,000 in foreign military financing to strengthen communications capabilities for the Republic of Fiji Navy, which Cavallo says will help Fiji track and disrupt transnational crime and illegal fishing in its waters.

The United States has also committed US$5.14 million over five years to strengthen Fiji’s ability to detect and contain infectious disease outbreaks.

Through the Millennium Challenge Corporation, the U.S. has also advanced a US$12 million grant to design and study a compact programme aimed at supporting Fiji’s long-term economic development.

Cavallo says U.S. State Department law enforcement assistance programmes, both through the U.S. Embassy in Fiji and Washington, also helped make the launch of the Counter Terrorism Strategy possible.

She says the United States remains committed to Fiji’s security and prosperity and to strengthening cooperation with its Pacific partners.

The strategy will run until 2030 and will be reviewed annually.

item.title: People urged to be vigilant after maggots found in BBQ bought from Valelevu roadside stall
item.description: People are being urged to be vigilant when buying food from roadside stalls after a couple found maggots in BBQ purchased from a stall in Valelevu, Nasinu, at around 1am today. The man has told fijivillage News he had already taken a few bites before discovering the maggots.
item.content:encoded:
People are being urged to be vigilant when buying food from roadside stalls after a couple found maggots in BBQ purchased from a stall in Valelevu, Nasinu, at around 1am today.

The man has told fijivillage News he had already taken a few bites before discovering the maggots.

Consumer Council of Fiji CEO Seema Shandil says finding maggots in food is a serious breach of food safety standards and indicates a possible breakdown in hygiene, storage or quality control.

Shandil says maggots in food are never normal and their presence may indicate that food has been contaminated or has been stale for several days.

She says roadside stalls and all food establishments have a responsibility to ensure the food they sell is safe, fit for purpose and fit for human consumption.

Shandil is advising consumers who find maggots in food to stop eating immediately and consider the entire product contaminated.

She says people should preserve the evidence by keeping the food in its original packaging where possible, taking clear photographs of the food, maggots and packaging, and keeping their receipt or proof of purchase.

She says people should also note the date, time and location of purchase and return to the retailer with the food, receipt and photographs to request a full refund or replacement.

Shandil says people should also report food safety concerns to the Consumer Council while concerns can also be reported to the Ministry of Health or the relevant Municipal Council.

Shandil says the food stalls in question operate after business hours and such matters are escalated to the Nasinu Town Council for inspection and any necessary enforcement action.

She says the Council is currently conducting surveillance of bakeries and restaurants and will soon extend this to roadside stalls.

However, Shandil says monitoring vendors who operate through the night and into the early morning hours presents significant challenges.

She is urging roadside food vendors to check their food, store it properly, protect it from flies and contamination, and throw away food that is not safe.

Questions have also been sent to the Nasinu Town Council.
